PART-II 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS 
1. Financial Allocation and Expenditure under NICRA 
The Committee observe that over the past five years, the National 
Innovations in Climate Resilient Agriculture (NICRA) project has seen a steady 
increase in both funding and spending for its demonstration and research 
activities. This shows the Government’s growing commitment to strengthening 
agricultural resilience against climate cha nge. The Committee note that  during 
2019-2024, the total allocation for NICRA was ₹231.85 crore and the total 
expenditure was ₹219.25 crore, which thus has been an impressive utilization 
rate of about 95%. While there were some small gaps between allocated  and 
used funds in the early years (88.2% in 2019 –20 and 89.8% in 2020 –21), the 
program has significantly improved, with utilization consistently exceeding 95% 
in recent years. This suggests that the planning, monitoring, and execution 
processes are gettin g better. The Committee also note that spending on 
research has consistently outpaced spending on demonstrations, which reflect 
a scientific and research -driven approach to building resilience. However, 
despite this efficiency, the limited budget has restr icted the scope of adaptation 
efforts, particularly in regions most vulnerable to climate change. 
 Further, the Committee observe that risk and vulnerability assessments 
have been conducted for 573 of the 651 agricultural districts in the country, as 
per t he guidelines of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). 
The assessments reveal that 109 districts are categorized as "very highly 
vulnerable" and 201 as "highly vulnerable," indicating that 310 districts are at 
significant risk from climate change. However, due to budget constraints, 
NICRA’s adaptation activities have only been implemented in only 151 of these 
high-risk districts, leaving a large number of vulnerable areas unaddressed. The 
Committee express their concern to note that so many regions are being 
neglected due to financial constraints, particularly when the very survival of 
agricultural livelihoods in these areas is at risk. This is a glaring shortfall, 
considering the scale of the challenges that these districts face.  
Given thes e limitations, the Committee strongly recommend that the 
Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare adopt a phased and rotational 

46 
 
approach to extend climate adaptation support to all 310 vulnerable districts. 
This approach would involve regularly reassess ing climate risks and ensuring 
that resources are directed to areas where they are most needed. Districts that 
show significant improvement in resilience could gradually transition out of the 
program, freeing up resources to focus on newly identified high -risk areas. The 
Committee feel that this phased approach would ensure that adaptation support 
is dynamic and can adjust to changing climatic conditions and evolving 
challenges over time. 
The Committee further recommend a substantial increase in funding for  
NICRA to effectively meet the scale of the challenges it seeks to address. The 
current budgetary allocation is woefully insufficient to address the scale of the 
crisis, and restrict the effectiveness of the program. Increased funding would 
not only allow for more region -specific interventions but would also enable the 
increase in of community -based resilience programmes, which are crucial for 
building long-term climate resilience at the grassroots level.  
The Committee also desire that the Ministry must en sure that funds are 
disbursed in a timely manner, with careful planning and active involvement from 
all relevant stakeholders. Inefficient fund distribution and delays in 
implementation can undermine the effectiveness of such programmes, limiting 
their pot ential impact. The Committee feel that, by ensuring prompt 
disbursement and active participation from local communities, the Ministry can 
significantly enhance the efficacy of NICRA and ensure that the programme 
delivers tangible benefits to farmers facing  climate-related challenges. Further, 
the Committee feel that, while the NICRA project has made commendable 
strides in strengthening agricultural resilience, the Ministry must address the 
glaring gaps in its reach and funding. A more comprehensive, well -funded, and 
dynamic approach with clear road map is needed to ensure that all vulnerable 
districts are supported and that climate resilience efforts are truly inclusive.  
2. Adoption of Climate-Resilient Seed Varieties 
The Committee are aware with the increasing frequency of droughts and 
floods, developing and disseminating climate -resilient seed varieties is 
important for helping farmers adapt to these changing conditions. Through the 
NICRA initiative, drought - and floo d-resistant varieties for crops such as rice, 

47 
 
wheat, and maize have been developed and introduced to farmers through 
Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs). However, the Committee note that significant 
challenges remain, including low farmer awareness, slow adoption  of new seed 
varieties, limited distribution networks, gaps in coordination at the state level, 
and the lack of large -scale assessments to measure the true impact of these 
efforts on agricultural resilience. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Min istry should prioritize 
improving seed distribution systems to ensure timely and easy access for 
farmers. The Committee feel that one effective way of doing this could be the 
establishment of decentralized seed hubs and the promotion of seed village 
programmes. These initiatives would improve the availability of climate -resilient 
seeds at the local level, making it easier for farmers to access them when 
needed most. In addition, the Committee are of the view that the Ministry should 
step up efforts to incre ase awareness among farmers regarding the benefits of 
these new seed varieties. This could be achieved through hands -on 
demonstrations, field trials involving farmers, and localized training 
programmes designed to suit specific climate conditions and farming practices.  
The Committee also feel that there is a need for increasing coordination 
between important stakeholders, such as the Indian Council of Agricultural 
Research (ICAR), state governments, seed companies, and other relevant 
agencies. Increased cooperation will ensure that climate -resilient seed varieties 
reach a wider group of farmers. Further, the Committee recommend that large -
scale assessments must be conducted to see how widely these varieties are 
being used and how they affect productivity an d resilience and to identify if 
there are  problems with implementation which can readily be addressed. To 
help farmers adopt these changes, the Committee also recommend that the 
Ministry should use digital tools to share information more easily. Mobile ap ps, 
SMS updates, community radio, and Agri -tech platforms can all help send 
important and timely information to farmers. Digital platforms can also provide 
valuable updates on seed availability, best practices for crop management, and 
current weather forec asts, all of which are crucial for farmers to adapt to the 
changing climate. The Committee are of the view that by implementing the 
aforementioned measures more farmers will adopt climate-resilient seeds.  

48 
 
3. Standardizing and Expanding Natural Farming 
The Committee note that Natural Farming (NF) is a chemical -free 
agricultural practice rooted in traditional Indian farming knowledge, integrating 
livestock with diverse crop systems. NF focuses on improving soil health, 
reducing input costs, and enhancing cli mate resilience. It relies on locally 
available on -farm resources, such as livestock and plants, without the use of 
purchased bio -fertilizers or mined minerals. The Committee also note that 
National Mission on Natural Farming (NMNF) is a centrally sponsore d initiative 
that collaborates with States and Union Territories to identify districts for 
implementation. The mission targets regions with varying levels of input use 
and areas where NF is already being practiced. Special priority is given to the 5 
km cor ridor along the Ganga under the Namami Gange program, as well as 
areas with strong traditional NF practices, experienced farmers, and supporting 
institutions like State Rural Livelihood Missions (SRLMs), Farmer Producer 
Organizations (FPOs), and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS). To help 
in the adoption of NF, model farms will be set up for training, demonstrations, 
and documentation, all tailored to local agro -ecological conditions. States 
actively involved in NF include Andhra Pradesh, Himachal  Pradesh, Gujarat, 
Kerala, Jharkhand, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, and 
Tamil Nadu. 
Given the diverse agricultural conditions across the country, the 
Committee feel that the Ministry must focus on standardizing NF while ensuring 
it remains adaptable to regional variations. The All India Network Programme on 
Organic Farming, which began in Kharif 2020, is testing NF practices across 
different agro-ecological settings in 16 states. The programme is focused on key 
NF techniques, such as con coctions (e.g., jeevamrit, beejamrit, and 
ghanjeevamrit), intercropping, mulching, and multi -variate crop -based green 
manuring during fallow periods. However, regional -specific factors —such as 
crop selection, varieties, mulching materials, trap crops, and traditional inputs—
must be carefully evaluated to ensure the practices are effective in local 
contexts. The Committee recommend that, based on the results of these 
experiments, a standardized yet flexible NF protocol should be developed in 
consultation wit h stakeholders, including farmers, agricultural experts, and 
local institutions. 

49 
 
The Committee feel that the Ministry need to expand NF efforts beyond 
the 5 km Ganga corridor. While this area is of significant importance, NF should 
be promoted in ecologically sensitive zones and areas facing high-input farming 
practices. Introducing NF in regions affected by soil degradation, water scarcity, 
and excessive chemical use can further enhance agricultural sustainability and 
climate resilience. The Committee are of the view that expanding NF to areas 
where soil health is compromised and where agricultural systems are heavily 
dependent on chemical inputs would be a transformative step toward 
sustainable farming. 
The Committee also feel that focusing on regions with  a solid foundation 
of NF practices, active farmer involvement, and strong local institutions is 
crucial for accelerating NF adoption. Strengthening training programmes and 
raising awareness through traditional and digital platforms will help farmers 
better understand the benefits of NF and encourage them to adopt which will 
improve agricultural productivity and environmental health. Collaboration with 
local farmers' organizations, rural development agencies, and other 
stakeholders will ensure the transitio n to NF is inclusive and sustainable.  
Further, the Committee are of the view that increasing the reach of NF, adapting 
it to local needs, and providing more resources and training will enable the 
Ministry to drive a nationwide shift toward more resilient, sustainable farming. 
The Committee also observed that KVKs in certain parts of country are 
primarily engaged in chemical farming, utilizing all available land, with little or 
no demonstrations on natural farming.  The Committee believe that farmers can 
truly understand the significant advantages of natural farming only if the KVKs 
take the initiative in promoting it. Therefore, the Committee recommend that the 
Ministry issue instructions to all KVKs to encourage natural farming in order to 
effectively communicate its benefits to the farming community. 
4. Enhancing Natural Farming Adoption 
The Committee note that the project "Out -Scaling of Natural Farming 
through Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs)" has made commendable progress by 
conducting 11,341 awareness programs that reached 11.37 lakh farmers and 
stakeholders. It also organised 2,476 training sessions for 1.02 lakh farmers and 
7,592 field demonstrations, providing valuable insights into the preparation of 
natural inputs like Beejamrit, Jeevamrit, and Ghanjeevamrit. These efforts have 
contributed to reduced cultivation costs (ranging from 3% to 55%), improved 
soil health, and better water retention in the soil. However, despite these 
promising results, concerns regarding stable income persist. While awareness 
and adoption have increased, financial security remains a significant barrier to 
the widespread adoption of Natural Farming (NF). 

50 
 
To address this, the Committee recommend that the Ministry should 
conduct a more detailed study among NF practitioners to track adoption rates, 
crop yields, and profitability. This study should gather data on th e long -term 
financial sustainability of NF, including cost savings, potential income 
improvements, and any challenges faced by farmers. The Committee feel that 
the results will provide a clearer understanding of the financial benefits of NF, 
helping to gui de future initiatives and ensure that the benefits of NF are both 
practical and financially viable for farmers. 
Further, the Committee recommend that the Ministry must focus on 
strengthening market linkages and developing premium pricing mechanisms for 
natural produce. As the demand for organic and natural produce is growing, and 
the Ministry should capitalize on this by connecting NF farmers with market 
players that are willing to pay a premium for their produce. Introducing support 
schemes, including fina ncial incentives and risk mitigation measures such as 
crop insurance or price guarantees, will help ease the financial risks involved in 
transitioning to NF. 
The Committee also recommend providing financial support, such as 
subsidies for input costs or low-interest loans for farmers transitioning to NF, to 
encourage wider adoption. These measures will help reduce the financial 
barriers that farmers face when shifting from chemical -based farming to natural 
farming. The Committee feel that with a clearer path way to financial security, 
more farmers are likely to adopt NF, ultimately leading to more sustainable and 
resilient farming systems across the country. 
5. Support Mechanism and Incentives for Organic Farming Transition 
The Committee observe that the Minis try has taken several commendable 
steps to support farmers transitioning from conventional to organic farming, 
such as the Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY), the Mission Organic 
Value Chain Development for the North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER), the PM -
PRANAM scheme, and the Financial Assistance through Direct Benefit Transfer 
(DBT) scheme. While these initiatives have yielded positive results, the 
Committee feel that a more robust and expanded support system is required to 
make the shift from convention al to organic farming more feasible and 
sustainable for farmers, particularly during the critical transition period. The 

51 
 
current financial support of ₹31,500 to ₹46,500 per hectare over three years, 
although a step in the right direction, might not be sufficient to fully alleviate the 
financial strain farmers experience during the first three to four years, a period 
in which yields tend to be lower and the economic burden heavier. 
To address this, the Committee recommend that the Ministry must 
increase the direct financial incentives under DBT for organic inputs and 
consider extending the support period beyond the current three years. This 
extended financial security will help ensure that farmers remain economically 
stable throughout the transition period. M oreover, to further strengthen market 
linkages, the Committee recommend that the Ministry invest in improving local 
marketing channels, enhance digital outreach, and establish premium pricing 
for organic products to make them more attractive to consumers a nd help 
farmers secure better returns for their produce. Strengthening platforms like the 
Jaivik Kheti portal, which has already benefited over 6.22 lakh farmers, would be 
an important step in this direction. The Committee also recommend reviewing 
and incr easing the current subsidy of ₹1,500 per metric ton (MT) under the 
Market Development Assistance (MDA) scheme to ensure that small and 
marginal farmers also benefit from this support. 
The Committee are also of the view that the PM -PRANAM scheme, which 
provides 50% of fertilizer subsidy savings to states that reduce chemical 
fertilizer use, should adopt a performance-based grants incentive structure. This 
would offer increased grants to states that make significant and sustained 
reductions in chemical fertil izer use, motivating a stronger shift toward 
sustainable farming practices. These performance -based grants should be 
allocated to capacity building, developing organic farming infrastructure, and 
creating local organic markets. The Committee believe that t his strategy will not 
only accelerate the adoption of organic farming but also promote long -term soil 
health, environmental sustainability, and economic stability for farming 
communities 
6. Sikkim Model of Organic Farming 
The Committee acknowledge the success of the Sikkim model, which 
highlights the potential of organic farming when supported by comprehensive 
strategies focused on increasing yields, reducing costs, improving market 

52 
 
access, and securing better pricing for o rganic produce. Notable successes of 
this model include stable productivity, improved soil health, and a shift towards 
high-value crops like cardamom, ginger, turmeric, and oranges. The emergence 
of "Organic Tourism" has also created new income opportuniti es for farmers. 
However, challenges such as high labour costs, difficult terrain, limited market 
access, and the shortage of essential organic inputs, particularly bio -fertilizers, 
continue to hinder profitability. The scarcity of quality bio -fertilizers r emains a 
significant concern, as it affects both productivity and the long -term 
sustainability of organic farming. 
To overcome these challenges and replicate the Sikkim model to other 
regions, the Committee recommend that the Ministry should enhance financ ial 
support for organic inputs, certification, and infrastructure development under 
schemes like the Mission Organic Value Chain Development for the North 
Eastern Region (MOVCDNER). The Ministry should focus on subsidizing labor -
intensive processes and addressing the shortage of bio-fertilizers. They  should 
also provide logistical support to overcome the challenges posed by difficult 
terrain, ensuring more efficient and reliable supply chains. In addition, the 
Committee also recommend the establishment of local bio-fertilizer production 
units to ensure a consistent and affordable supply of organic inputs. This would 
reduce reliance on external sources and help lower overall farming costs. The 
Ministry should also focus on strengthening market linkages, both  online and 
offline, and create dedicated organic retail outlets in urban centers to improve 
market access and ensure fair pricing for organic produce. To formalize fair 
pricing, the Committee recommend that the existing 20 –30% premium for 
organic products  be institutionalized through a system of minimum support 
prices (MSP) for key organic crops, ensuring that farmers are adequately 
compensated for their efforts. 
The Committee feel that eco -tourism is a valuable opportunity to support 
organic farming by gi ving farmers extra income. Adding organic farm visits to 
tourism packages could attract tourists, both local and international, and raise 
awareness about organic farming. This would help farmers earn more money 
and create greater demand for organic product s. The Committee are of the view 
that linking farming with tourism, organic farming can gain more recognition 
and benefit both farmers and the local community. 

53 
 
7. Strengthening Organic Certification and Market Access for Farmers 
The Committee recognize the  significant role played by the Ministry in 
implementing two key certification systems — the National Programme for 
Organic Production (NPOP) and the Participatory Guarantee System (PGS -
India)—to promote organic food quality in India. NPOP, managed by the Ministry 
of Commerce, is aimed at both domestic and export markets with third -party 
certification, while PGS -India, managed by the Ministry of Agriculture, is a 
decentralized, cost -effective, farmer -centric system tailored to the domestic 
market. Together, these systems have contributed greatly to the growth of 
organic agriculture in India, ensuring compliance with organic standards and 
increasing transparency in the market. 
However, the Committee feel that there are opportunities to improve the 
certification processes, especially to make them more accessible for small-scale 
farmers. While NPOP and PGS -India have proven effective, the certification 
procedures can be complex and expensive, posing a significant barrier for 
smaller farmers. The Committee recomme nd that the Ministry must explore 
ways to simplify the certification process, including reducing paperwork, 
lowering certification costs, and providing financial assistance or subsidies, 
particularly for farmers using the PGS -India system. PGS-India, being designed 
for small-scale producers, can benefit from these adjustments, but NPOP also 
needs to be made more accessible for smaller operations. The Ministry should 
consider introducing tiered certification models under NPOP, which would make 
it easier for small farmers to access markets and receive premium prices for 
their organic products. 
To further improve the organic certification process, the Committee 
recommend the Ministry to establish a unified organic label for both NPOP and 
PGS-India certified products. This would create consistency in marketing, 
enhance consumer confidence, and sim plify the identification of authentic 
organic products. The Committee also desire that the Ministry should focus on 
simplifying the certification procedure, by reducing costs, and exploring digital 
solutions to streamline the application process and monito ring, ensuring 
accessibility for small farmers. The Committee feel that this comprehensive 

54 
 
approach would not only improve the certification process but also promote 
transparency and foster greater trust in India’s organic products. 
The Committee also feel that, despite the availability of these certification 
systems, many farmers may still not fully understand their benefits or the 
certification process itself. The Committee, therefore, recommend the Ministry 
to increase awareness campaigns to educate farm ers—particularly in rural 
areas—about the importance of certification and its long -term advantages. 
Further, the Committee desire that the Ministry should explore the possibility of 
fully digitizing the certification process for both NPOP and PGS -India. An online 
platform could streamline the application process, reduce paperwork, increase 
transparency, and make it easier for farmers to track their certification status. A 
digital system could also facilitate remote inspections or audits, especially in 
areas with limited access to certification bodies, enabling more efficient and 
cost-effective monitoring. 
8. Cold Storage infrastructure for perishable Crops 
The Ministry has made notable progress in addressing storage losses, 
particularly for perishable crops like onions, through the development of 
controlled atmosphere storage facilities under the Public -Private Partnership 
(PPP) model. The Controlled Atmosphere Onion and Multi -Product Storage 
Facility has proven successful, maintaining optimal conditions (tem perature at 
27 ± 2°C and relative humidity at 60 -65%) and significantly reducing storage 
losses to less than 15%, compared to the 40 -60% losses typically seen with 
traditional storage methods. The Committee also note that CONCOR (Container 
Corporation of I ndia) has been involved in improving the transportation of 
perishable goods by providing refrigerated container logistics. This partnership 
has increased the efficiency of moving stored products to market while 
preserving quality. However, the Committee no te that the adoption and 
availability of such facilities for other perishable crops, such as fruits, 
vegetables, and high -value crops like tomatoes, potatoes, and leafy greens, 
remain limited. 
The Committee recommend that the successful model of the onion 
storage facility developed by ICAR -DOGR and Kala Biotech be replicated and 
scaled up for a wider range of perishable crops. The Committee feel that 

55 
 
expanding controlled atmosphere storage for various crops would help reduce 
post-harvest losses significantl y. The Committee desire that the Government 
should work closely with the private sector to expand these facilities, 
prioritizing high-production areas where storage losses are the most significant. 
To further encourage private sector participation in build ing cold storage 
infrastructure, the Committee desire that the Government should explore the 
possibilities of providing financial incentives, such as subsidies, tax breaks, or 
low-interest loans, specifically aimed at the establishment of controlled 
atmosphere storage facilities. These incentives would help reduce the financial 
burden on private stakeholders and encourage them to build more storage units 
in rural and peri -urban areas, thereby benefitting small farmers who currently 
lack adequate storage options. 
The Committee also acknowledge that different crops have varying 
requirements when it comes to temperature and humidity for optimal storage. 
To address this, the Committee recommend the Ministry to initiate research into 
crop-specific controlled atmo sphere storage technologies that are required to 
the unique needs of various fruits, vegetables, and grains. This would ensure 
that cold storage facilities are designed for maximum efficiency and quality 
preservation across diverse crops. 
The Committee als o desire that the Ministry must prioritize cold storage 
infrastructure development in rural and remote areas, especially in regions with 
high horticultural production. These units should be specifically designed as 
net zero controlled cold storage atmosphe re houses. This will not only save 
carbon emission but will reduce the cost of storage of perishable goods. This 
will help small scale farmer by reducing post -harvest losses. The Ministry also 
needs to collaborate with Ministry of New and Renewable under PM Surya Ghar 
Scheme for energy solutions and other related benefits. Further, the Committee 
recommend the Ministry to expand the PPP model used for onion storage to 
include multi-crop storage facilities. In this model, the Government could act as 
a facilitator by providing land, subsidies, and technical support, while the 
private sector manages the operations. This partnership approach would help 
maximize resource utilization and ensure the availability of efficient cold storage 
facilities across the country, ultimately benefiting both farmers and consumers 
by reducing food wastage and improving market access. 

56 
 
9. Promoting Efficient Fertilizer Use and Distribution Systems 
The C ommittee note the adverse effects of excessive and imbalanced 
fertilizer use on soil health, crop productivity, and livestock nutrition. The 
Committee also note about the Ministry's ongoing efforts to address these 
issues, through research and the promotio n of integrated nutrient management 
(INM). The use of soil test based nutrient application and a mix of organic and 
inorganic sources has been found to help maintain soil fertility and improve 
sustainability. 
In their submission, the Ministry explained tha t fertilizer distribution from 
manufacturers to farmers is monitored through an online process. The system 
will soon be fully digitized, including the sale of fertilizers from licensed 
manufacturers to retailers, to increase transparency. Efforts are also being 
made to generate online receipts, which will address issues like missing 
receipts due to GST -related problems, making the process smoother for both 
retailers and farmers. Any transaction that occurs outside of this system will be 
considered unauthorized, ensuring stricter control over fertilizer distribution. 
In order to increase efficiency in fertilizer use, the Committee feel that the 
Ministry must intensify efforts to promote soil test -based nutrient management, 
and advocate for balanced fertilizer  use, incorporating organic matter, and 
improving nutrient delivery methods. Modern approaches like precision nutrient 
management should be encouraged to make fertilizer use more efficient and 
reduce dependency on chemical fertilizers. Further, the Ministr y should focus 
on developing and promoting climate -resilient crop varieties that require fewer 
nutrients, ensuring more sustainable agricultural practices. The Committee 
desire that the Ministry should develop a clear action plan, with specific 
timeframes to promote the large -scale adoption of these practices, and regular 
impact assessments should be conducted to evaluate their effectiveness in 
improving soil health, sustaining crop yields, and minimizing environmental 
harm. 
The Committee appreciate the Min istry’s move towards an online system 
for fertilizer distribution, which enhances transparency and helps prevent 
unauthorized transactions. However, considering the challenges in areas with 
limited internet access and among marginal farmers who may lack di gital 
literacy, the system may face obstacles, cause delays or errors in fertilizer 

57 
 
distribution in such areas.  The Committee therefore urge the Ministry to put in 
place contingency plans to manage potential technical issues and ensure the 
continuous flow  of fertilizer distribution. Capacity -building initiatives should 
also be rolled out to help farmers, retailers, and other stakeholders to better 
navigate the online system. In addition, a real -time monitoring and grievance 
redressal system should be set u p to address any issues related to fertilizer 
transactions and ensure quick resolution of any discrepancies.  
10. Promotion and Adoption of Nano Fertilizers  
The Committee note that the promotion of Nano Fertilizers is actively 
being pursued through variou s initiatives aimed at reducing the reliance on 
traditional fertilizers while improving agricultural productivity. These efforts 
include awareness campaigns, webinars, street plays ( nukkad nataks ), field 
demonstrations, Kisan Sammelans, and regional -language films, all designed to 
educate farmers about the benefits of Nano Fertilizers. These fertilizers are 
available at Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samridhi Kendras (PMKSKs) and are included 
in the monthly supply plan issued by the Department of Fertilizers. The Ind ian 
Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) has also conducted a national 
campaign on the "Efficient and Balanced Use of Fertilizer," which highlights 
Nano Fertilizers. This campaign is supported under the Viksit Bharat Sankalp 
Yatra (VBSY), launched in November 2023. 
The Committee appreciate the innovative efforts to facilitate the use of 
Nano Fertilizers, including the use of agricultural drones operated by women 
from Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and battery -operated sprayers, available at retail 
points. The Central Sector Scheme "NAMO Drone Didi," approved by the 
Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), has provided 1,094 drones in 
its first phase to women in SHGs, enabling a broader application of Nano 
Fertilizers using drone technology. This initiative  has the potential to make 
Nano Fertilizers more accessible and practical for farmers, especially in rural 
areas. 
In response to the Committee’s concerns about reducing reliance on 
traditional fertilizers, the Ministry shared results from field studies conducted by 
ICAR-IARI, which showed that Nano Fertilizers can reduce nitrogen use by up to 
25%. The study demonstrat ed that two sprays of Nano -N could achieve the 
same results as the recommended nitrogen dose, pointing to potential cost 

58 
 
savings. However, the Ministry also acknowledged the need for further research 
to fully understand the long -term benefits of Nano Ferti lizers, particularly in 
terms of nutrient budgeting. 
The Committee feel that Nano Fertilizers can offer substantial savings for 
farmers. Since only half a litre of Nano Fertilizer can deliver the same results as 
five kilograms of traditional fertilizer, fa rmers can significantly reduce costs. 
This also has the added benefit of reducing India’s dependence on fertilizer 
imports, contributing to national savings. However, the Committee feel that the 
message about the potential savings and environmental benefit s of Nano 
Fertilizers has not been adequately communicated to farmers. Much more needs 
to be done to raise awareness about these advantages. 
To address this, the Committee recommend that the Ministry take urgent 
action to improve outreach and communication  about Nano Fertilizers. This 
should include expanding awareness campaigns, creating clear and easy -to-
understand educational materials in local languages, and conducting hands -on 
training programmes that directly engage farmers, especially in rural and 
remote areas. The Ministry should also focus on establishing more local 
distribution channels for Nano Fertilizers, ensuring that they are easily 
accessible to farmers. Further, the Ministry must intensify efforts to 
communicate the cost -saving potential of Nano Fertilizers, ensuring that 
farmers fully understand how they can lower their fertilizer expenses. The 
Committee feel that these efforts are crucial not only for maximizing the benefits 
of Nano Fertilizers but also for achieving long -term agricultural sustainability 
and reducing India’s reliance on imported fertilizers. 
11. Safe Pest Management Practices and Promoting Non-Chemical Alternatives 
The Committee expressed serious concerns about the excessive use of 
pesticides and sought clarification from th e Ministry on the measures being 
taken to ensure their safe and responsible use. In response, the Ministry 
explained that pesticide recommendations, approved by the Central Insecticide 
Board & Registration Committee (CIB&RC), are based on extensive multi -year 
trials conducted through the All India Coordinated Research Projects (AICRP). 
These trials focus on specific pest -crop combinations across different regions. 
The resulting recommendations are incorporated into state specific agricultural 
practices afte r being validated through Adaptive Trials on farmers' fields. The 

59 
 
Ministry also highlighted efforts to promote registered bio -pesticides as safer 
alternatives to chemical pesticides. However, the Committee expressed 
dissatisfaction with the Ministry's inab ility to effectively implement these 
recommendations, leading to continued overuse of pesticides, which remains a 
significant issue. 
The Committee are of the view that an effective and coordinated 
approach, involving state governments and other stakeholder s, is crucial to 
curbing the widespread and often irresponsible use of pesticides. The 
Committee believe that this requires not only stricter implementation of CIB&RC 
recommendations but also a concerted effort to raise awareness among farmers 
about the sa fe application of pesticides. Regular training sessions, television 
broadcasts, and radio programmes could help disseminate this knowledge more 
widely. 
The Committee are also of the view that there is an urgent need to 
increase adoption of biological pest management technologies developed by 
the ICAR -National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources (NBAIR) as a 
sustainable alternative to chemical pesticides. The Committee are concerned 
about the persistently high levels of pesticide residues found in variou s food 
products like vegetables, grains, fruits, and animal feed, which pose serious 
health risks, including cancer and other life -threatening diseases. While the 
Ministry acknowledged the need for promoting good agricultural practices, 
educating farmers a bout recommended pesticide dosages, encouraging bio -
pesticide use, and integrating pest management practices, the Committee feel 
that these efforts have not been effective in reducing harmful pesticide residue 
levels. 
The Ministry also informed the Committ ee about the Monitoring of 
Pesticide Residues at the National Level (MPRNL) project, which has been 
running since 2005 -06. This project monitors pesticide residues through 35 
participating laboratories across multiple institutions, including the Ministry o f 
Agriculture, ICAR, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Environment, CSIR, Ministry of 
Chemicals and Fertilizers, and State Agricultural Universities. The data 
generated from this project is shared with state agriculture departments to 
guide farmers in the sa fe use of pesticides. However, the Committee expressed 
disappointment that despite these initiatives, pesticide residues continue to be 

60 
 
detected in various food products such as vegetables, fruits, spices, cereals, 
meat, eggs, milk, fish, tea and marine products. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend the Ministry to take immediate and 
effective action to ensure that the recommendations of CIB&RC are better 
implemented, with visible results on the ground. It is essential to reduce harmful 
pesticide residues and protect both public health and agricultural produce from 
contamination. To this end, the Committee recommend that the Ministry review 
and strengthen the enforcement of provisions under the Insecticides Act, 1968. 
The Committee feel that a more robust enf orcement mechanism is needed to 
prevent the excessive and harmful use of pesticides, ensuring compliance with 
safety guidelines and mitigating associated health risks. 
12. Preventing the Use of Fake Pesticides and Insecticides 
The Committee raised serious concerns about the widespread issue of 
counterfeit pesticides and their harmful effects on agriculture. They sought 
clarification from the Ministry on the measures being taken to address this 
problem and protect agricultural produce from the damage caused by fake 
pesticides.  In response, the Ministry outlined the existing regulatory framework 
under the Insecticides Act, 1968 , where the Registration Committee (RC), a 
technical body, evaluates the safety and effectiveness of pesticides. The RC has 
established comprehensive guidelines covering chemistry, bio-efficacy, toxicity, 
packaging, and legal standards to ensure the quality of pesticides. The Ministry 
also informed the Committee that there are 11,080 state -level Insecticide 
Inspectors across 25 states an d 2 Union Territories, with an annual testing 
capacity of 77,040 samples. The Central Government deploys 207 Central 
Insecticide Inspectors, and there are two Regional Pesticide Testing 
Laboratories in Chandigarh and Kanpur with a combined annual capacity of 
3,100 samples. Any disputed samples are sent to the Central Insecticides 
Laboratory (CIL) in Faridabad, which processes 1,600 samples annually. If 
samples fail to meet the required standards, prosecution is initiated. 
 The Committee are of the view that there is a need to increase the number 
of Insecticide Inspectors at the state level and strengthening the capacity of 
overseeing officers at the central level. They also emphasized the need to 
expand and improve testing facilities, both in terms of quanti ty and quality, to 
ensure better monitoring and control of pesticide quality. 

61 
 
The Committee also note that the penalties for offences related to 
"misbranded" insecticides under Section 29 of the Insecticides Act, 1968, are 
insufficient to deter offenders. The Committee find that, between 2019 -2020 and 
2023-2024, out of 3,60,614 samples analyzed, 9,233 were found to be 
misbranded, leading to 2,588 prosecutions and only 185 convictions. The 
Committee are very concerned over the low conviction rate and stresse d the 
urgent need for stronger regulations to tackle violations under the Insecticides 
Act. The Committee recommend tightening regulations to curb the production, 
distribution, and use of counterfeit pesticides by amending the Insecticides Act, 
1968 to include provisions for stringent penalties to ensure repeat offenders are 
held accountable. 
13.  District-Wise Ranking of KVKs 
The Committee note that in 2018, the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' 
Welfare (MoA&FW) commissioned a third -party evaluation of Krishi Vigyan 
Kendras (KVKs) through the National Institute of Labour Economics Research 
and Development (NILERD), an autonomous organization of NITI Aayog. This 
evaluation focused on KVKs established during the XII Five -Year Plan (2012 -
2017), examining factors like infrastructure, impact, and the quality of activities. 
The findings show that 43% of KVKs were placed in the A category, 48% in the B 
category, while 8% and 1% were in the C and D categories, respectively. The 
underperformance of KVKs in the C a nd D categories was attributed to 
challenges like vacant staff positions and incomplete infrastructure, particularly 
in newly established centers that were still under development. 
The Committee also note that the last ranking of KVKs was conducted 
during the XII Five -Year Plan, and no subsequent evaluations have been done. 
This has created a gap in tracking KVK performance and providing appropriate 
support. Without regular updates, it is difficult to assess whether KVKs in lower 
categories have improved or continue to face the same challenges. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry must implement a 
district-wise ranking system for KVKs periodically for a more precise and 
effective performance assessment. The Committee desire that this system 
should categorize KVKs not just based on overall performance but also evaluate 
them according to specific subject areas, productivity, and impact on local 
farming communities. The Committee feel that a district -wise approach is 

62 
 
important as it helps provid e help based on each KVK’s unique needs and 
strengths. It will allow for better tracking of region -specific issues and ensures 
that the Ministry can respond to the unique needs of farmers in different areas.  
The Committee also feel that district -wise rank ing system will also help 
identify high-performing KVKs, which can then be incentivized for their success, 
further motivating them to maintain their standards and share best practices 
with other centers. It will also highlight underperforming KVKs, particu larly 
those in the C and D categories, so they can receive focused support, whether 
it's through staffing, infrastructure, or training. The ranking system would also 
allow for continuous monitoring, making it easier to track improvements and 
assess whether the resources allocated are being effectively utilized. 
The Committee are of the view that regular rankings will ensure 
accountability, providing greater transparency and enabling the Ministry to 
assess KVK performance over time. This will create a system  of healthy 
competition among KVKs and offer a clear picture of where further 
improvements are needed. This will not only help the Ministry monitor and 
support KVKs more effectively but also empower farmers to access the most 
relevant, timely, and effective support available. 
14. Ensuring Effectiveness of KVKs through Regular Performance Reviews 
The Committee appreciate the periodic third -party evaluations of KVKs 
conducted by various institutions such as the High-Level Committee (2015), NITI 
Aayog, NILERD(2017-18), IFPRI (2019), and ISAPs (2021 -22). These evaluations 
have shown positive results, including an additional net farm income of Rs. 
5,752 per hectare and a benefit cost ratio of 11.78, as reported by IFPRI. The 
ISAPs evaluation highlighted the succe ss of on -farm trials, frontline 
demonstrations, and Integrated Farming Systems (IFS) models. The Committee 
note that feedback from farmers pointed to a strong demand for more 
demonstrations of precision agriculture, improved farm tools, and technologies 
to reduce drudgery. There was also a call for KVKs to play a more prominent 
role in promoting entrepreneurship through Agri -clinics and agri -business 
supply systems. 
In the light of these findings, the Committee recommend that KVK 
performance may be regularl y evaluated to ensure that their programmes 
remain relevant and effective in addressing the evolving challenges of 

63 
 
agriculture. These evaluations should not only focus on quantitative outcomes, 
like net farm income and benefit -cost ratios, but also on qual itative aspects 
such as the impact on sustainability, soil health, and climate -resilient practices. 
The Committee feel that KVKs should place greater emphasis on showcasing 
innovative technologies, such as precision farming, climate smart agriculture, 
and tools that reduce farm labour. The Committee also stress the importance of 
promoting entrepreneurship, especially in Agri -clinics and agri -business 
ventures, and encourages stronger collaboration with local research 
institutions, NGOs, and farmer producer organizations (FPOs) to ensure the 
programs meet the real needs of the farming community. 
15. Need for Adequate and Consistent Funding for KVKs 
 The Committee observed from the Revised Estimates (RE) provided by 
the Ministry for Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) over the last five years that while 
the budget allocation has seen an increase, the funding trajectory remains 
insufficient for the growing demands and challenges KVKs face. The budget 
allocation increased from Rs. 22,298.47 lakhs in 2019 -20 to Rs. 28,400.00 lakhs 
in 2021 -22. However, this increase was followed by a slight decrease to Rs. 
24,372.00 lakhs in 2022 -23 and only a marginal rise to Rs. 25,000.00 lakhs in 
2023-24. While the Ministry highlights this as a positive movement, the reality is 
that the funding still falls short of what is needed to meet the evolving demands 
of KVKs, especially as they continue to face pressure for improved 
infrastructure, technology, and capacity-building to support farmers effectively. 
 Despite this gradual increase, the Ministry’s proposal for a one -time grant 
of Rs. 2,500 crores to address capital expenditure and staff enhancement needs 
seem to indicate ongoing challenges KVKs face in securing sufficient funds for 
infrastructure development and other essential. T he Committee feel that this 
one-time grant is merely a short -term patch and does not address the 
underlying issue of underfunding. The resources currently available are clearly 
insufficient to meet the growing needs of KVKs to modernize their infrastructur e 
and adopt new technologies. 
 The Committee feel that the Ministry need to establish a robust and 
consistent funding strategy with long -term vision for the development of KVKs. 
While the proposed one -time grant of Rs. 2,500 crores may provide some 

64 
 
immediate relief, it cannot serve as a substitute for predictable, annual funding 
increases that reflect the evolving needs of KVKs. The current funding model 
appears to be reactionary rather than proactive, and the Committee are 
concerned that such piecemeal inc reases will leave KVKs unable to keep pace 
with infrastructure and technological demands, as well as their increasing 
responsibilities in supporting farmers. 
 The Committee strongly recommend that the Ministry move beyond short-
term fixes and commit to a s ustainable, long-term funding plan for KVKs. The 
funding increases must be substantial, consistent, and in tune with the evolving 
needs of KVKs. This approach is essential to ensure that KVKs remain viable, 
effective, and relevant as centers of agricultural innovation and training. 
   The Committee also recommend that a significant portion of the funding 
should be allocated to infrastructure development, including modernizing 
laboratories, procuring advanced agricultural technologies, and establishing 
digital platforms for efficient knowledge dissemination.  Further, the Committee 
also desire that a robust monitoring mechanism should be established to 
ensure that allocated funds are used efficiently and transparently. Regular 
audits, progress reviews, and impact assessments will enabl e the Ministry to 
track the effectiveness of the funds, ensuring they have the desired impact on 
KVK operations. The Committee feel that, this oversight is crucial to maintain 
accountability and ensure that the funding is being utilized to meet the growing  
needs of agricultural development. 
 16. Standardization of Service Conditions across all KVKs 
The Committee note that the service conditions of KVK employees are 
determined by the respective employer/host organizations as per the approved 
KVK Scheme by th e Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) for a 
period of five years (or Plan period) through the Expenditure Finance Committee 
(EFC). The ICAR serves as the nodal agency for the implementation of the KVK 
Scheme. The guidelines of the KVK Scheme are s trictly implemented as per the 
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and the sanction order issued by ICAR, 
in compliance with the Rules and Bye-Laws of ICAR. 

65 
 
The Committee further note that ICAR does not directly pay the salary and 
allowances of KVK employees . There is no employer -employee relationship 
between ICAR and the employees of non -ICAR KVKs. The limited connection is 
that the host organizations, other than ICAR, which are the actual employers of 
KVK employees in non-ICAR KVKs, pay the salaries and allowances through the 
grant-in-aid received from ICAR, as per the terms of the MoU, the sanction 
order, and the guidelines under the KVK Scheme and Government of India 
Rules. 
The Committee expressed serious concerns about the lack of 
standardization in the s ervice conditions and operational guidelines across 
Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) due to the varying host organizations. This 
inconsistency in service conditions has led to disparities in employee benefits 
and operational procedures, which, if left unaddres sed, could negatively impact 
the morale and effectiveness of KVK employees. The service conditions for 
employees in ICAR KVKs differ from those in non -ICAR KVKs, creating an 
unequal work environment. The Ministry, during their oral submissions, have 
also a ssured the Committee that the issue of disparities in service conditions 
among KVKs is being actively addressed, and necessary corrective measures 
are being incorporated.  
The Committee are of the view that the disparities between the service 
conditions and benefits offered to employees of ICAR and non -ICAR KVKs have 
created a significant divide, leading to potential dissatisfaction and a decrease 
in employee morale. These discrepancies have the potential to hinder the 
productivity and success of KVKs acros s the country. The absence of 
uniformity in employee benefits, staff roles, promotion policies, and other 
critical aspects reflects a lack of coherence in the operation of the KVK Scheme. 
This inconsistency not only affects employee satisfaction but also r aises 
concerns about the overall efficiency of KVKs in fulfilling their objectives. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry must urgently 
address these disparities and establish standardized service conditions across 
all KVKs. To resolve this issue, the Committee recommend revising the terms of 
the MoU governing non -ICAR KVKs, particularly those hosted by State 
Agricultural Universities (SAUs) and other organizations. These revisions 
should ensure that service conditions and benefits are broug ht in line with 

66 
 
those provided to ICAR KVK employees. SAUs should extend the same benefits 
to KVK employees as those provided to state government employees, and other 
host organizations should be required to provide same service conditions 
accordingly. The  Committee also recommend that the uniformity in service 
conditions be made a mandatory pre -condition for any host organization to 
receive grant-in-aid from ICAR. The Committee desire that the Ministry should 
take swift and decisive action to create a fair , consistent, and cohesive working 
environment for all KVK employees across the country. 
17. Need for Staff Augmentation at KVKs 
 The Committee are deeply concerned about the critical staff shortages at 
Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs), with approximately 30% of positions unfilled, 
totaling around 3,500 vacancies. This staff shortfall is significantly impairing the 
KVKs' ability to effec tively carry out their core functions, which include 
providing expert guidance, conducting training programmes, supporting 
research, and facilitating the adoption of new agricultural technologies.  The 
Committee note that the  Ministry has proposed to incr ease staff numbers from 
16 to 20 per KVK . The Committee feel that while this is a welcome step, it will 
not be effective unless vacancies are filled promptly.  
 The Committee strongly recommend that the Ministry must initiate an 
immediate recruitment driv e to fill the existing vacancies with a focus to hiring 
qualified professionals, such as Subject Matter Specialists (SMS) and Technical 
Assistants (T-3), who are essential for providing farmers with expert advice on a 
range of agricultural issues, from cro p management to soil health. These 
professionals are also crucial for facilitating the transfer of technology from 
research to practical applications on the ground.  
In addition to filling vacancies, the Committee feel that KVKs need staff 
with expertise i n emerging agricultural technologies. Positions such as 
Precision Agriculture Specialists, Agricultural Data Analysts, and Tech Support 
Staff are essential for helping farmers adopt tools like AI, remote sensing, and 
precision farming. Multi -skilled roles should also be created to allow staff to 
address a wider range of challenges, from research to farmer outreach. 
The Committee also desire that the Ministry should undertake a review of 
the current staff roles to enhance efficiency. There may be areas of ov erlap or 

67 
 
tasks that can be streamlined to help KVKs operate more effectively with the 
existing workforce. For example, scientists could take on additional 
responsibilities, such as creating digital content for online training, as virtual 
platforms become more prevalent.  Further, the Committee recommend that the 
Ministry should create a long term staffing plan that anticipates the evolving 
needs of KVKs. This plan should be based on workload data, technology 
adoption, and regional challenges. Regular review s of staffing levels will also 
ensure that KVKs are adequately equipped to meet both current and future 
demands. Further, the Ministry should explore the possibility of associating 
expert staff, research fellows, and senior students from Central and State 
Agricultural Universities to assist in imparting trainings at KVKs. This approach 
could not only address the issue of staff shortages at KVKs but also ensure that 
the training programmes remain aligned with the latest trends and 
advancements in sustainable agriculture. 
18. Harnessing AI and digital Tech in Agriculture 
 The Committee commends the Ministry’s efforts through NICRA (National 
Innovations in Climate Resilient Agriculture) in addressing the challenges 
climate change poses to agriculture. Through t he development of climate -
resilient crop varieties, comprehensive risk assessments, and capacity -building 
programmes, NICRA has significantly enhanced farmers' ability to adapt to 
changing climatic conditions. Further, the Ministry's commitment to integrat ing 
digital technologies, particularly AI -driven predictive models, is a significant 
step forward and should be further supported and expanded to maximize its 
potential benefits. 
 The Committee are of the view that using AI and machine learning in 
agriculture can greatly benefit farmers by providing real -time information on 
weather patterns, pest outbreaks, and crop health. AI -based early warning 
systems can help farmers prepare for extreme weather events like floods or 
droughts, and quickly respond to pest  issues, reducing losses and improving 
resilience.  AI can also work with precision farming to optimize resource use, 
such as water, fertilizers, and pesticides, leading to better sustainability and 
higher productivity. 

68 
 
 As AI technology continues to evolve, the Committee recommend that the 
Ministry should explore partnerships with tech companies, agricultural 
universities, and research institutions. These collaborations could help make AI 
tools more accessible to farmers in remote and disadvantaged areas, ensuring 
that all farmers, regardless of location, can benefit from these innovations. It is 
essential for Ministry to ensure that AI tools are both affordable and user -
friendly to increase their adoption. The Ministry should also focus on providing 
training programmes to equip farmers with the skills needed to effectively use 
AI technologies. This will empower farmers to make the most of these 
advancements, ensuring they can improve their farm practices. Further, the 
Committee feel that it is important to ensure that the necessary infrastructure, 
such as reliable internet and mobile connectivity, is available in rural areas to 
support these technologies. 
19. “Lab to Land” Initiatives 
 The Committee are happy to note that the “Lab to Land” initiatives under 
ICAR and the Central Agricultural Universities (CAUs) have made a significant 
impact in improving agricultural productivity and promoting climate -resilient 
farming practices.  Institutions such as the Central Agricultural University 
(Imphal), RPCAU (Pusa) and Rani Lakshmi Bai Central Agricultural University 
(Jhansi) have successfully translated research into practical solutions that 
directly benefit farmers.  Through field trials, demonstrations and localized 
adaptations of research, these initiatives have contributed to increasing 
farmers’ access to modern technologies and improved farming methods. 
 However, the Committee are of the view that, while the initial 
demonstrations and trials have shown positive outcomes, consistent follow -up 
support is important  for the long -term adoption of these new practices.  Many 
farmers face challenges when transitioning to new technologies and without 
continuous support, they may struggle to fully implement or maintain these 
practices.  The Committee recommend that there m ust be regular follow -ups by 
extension officers, Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) staff and field experts who can 
address the issues farmers might be facing such as pest control, weather -
related challenges and technological difficulties.  The Committee feel that  
establishing a system where farmers can access continuous guidance, through 
in-person visits, phone consultations or digital platforms, would significantly 

69 
 
enhance the effectiveness of the “Lab to Land” initiatives.  Such a system will 
help build farmers’  confidence and ensure the continuity of the new practices 
being introduced. 
 The Committee also recommend that successful pilot projects and 
innovations resulting from these initiatives must be augmented to reach a large 
number of farmers.  Expanding the scope of these trails and rolling out 
innovations on a broader scale will maximize their impact and benefit a greater 
number of agricultural communities.  For augmenting these innovations, the 
Committee feel that it is essential to foster stronger collabor ation between 
research institutions, government bodies, and the private sector.  Public -Private 
Partnerships can facilitate the wider dissemination of research outcome and 
help integrate innovative technologies into farming systems more effectively. 
 The C ommittee are of the view that promoting farmer -to-farmer 
knowledge exchange is a valuable way to strengthen the impact of these 
initiatives.  Farmers who have successfully adopted new technologies can serve 
as mentors or lead demonstrations for others in t heir communities, promoting a 
grassroots approach to adoption and adaption.  The Committee feel that peer -
learning model will be effective in rural areas, where trust and community-based 
collaboration are strong.

Climate Resilient Agriculture, Natural and Organic Farming through KVKs’. The ir

subject followed b y a brief introduction on Natural and Organic Farming by the 
Secretary, Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. The presentation 
highlighted the climate resilient technologies to minimize climatic stresses, flood 
tolerant improved crop varieties, st rategies for improving fodder availability, 
interventions for livestock, integrated farming systems, promotion of natural farming 
and their demonstrations through KVKs, capacity development of scientists, science of 
intercropping/multi-cropping and using concoctions, etc. 
 
4.  The Chairperson and other Members of the Committee, then raised several 
queries relating to the subject. The queries inter alia  were related to government 
initiatives to promote natural and organic farming, strategies to enhance yields in

disadvantages of overuse of fertilizers, pesticides and insecticides , promotion of nano 
fertilizers, commercialization of bio -fertilizers, increasing funding of KVKs under 
various heads, pay parity of all types of KVK employees, imparting more trainings with 
farmers by KVKs, providing comprehensive data on soil sample testing, etc.

3.  Dr. Himanshu Pathak, Secretary (DARE) & DG ICAR made a presentation 
focusing on t he challenges posed by climate change on agriculture. He emphasized 
strategies to address extreme weather conditions such as heavy rainfall, storms, 
droughts, heatwaves, and cold stress. Dr. Pathak also outlined initiatives like on -site 
demonstrations and capacity-building programs for farmers, the development of 
climate-resistant crop varieties, soil testing, nutrition management for livestock, and 
the breeding of new poultry and piggery varieties  as well as an update on the 
progress of natural farming an d organic farming through KVKs. Shri Devesh 
Chaturvendi, Secretary of the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, briefed 
the Committee on the status of service conditions for KVKs employees. He discussed 
the coordination of KVKs with state agricult ure departments and the usage of land 
under KVKs. 
 
4.  The Chairperson and members the Committee, then raised several queries 
related to the subject. These included concerns about the impact of urban 
infrastructure development on agriculture, the timely is suance of weather forecasts, 
and district -wise impact evaluations of the National Initiative on Climate Resilient 
Agriculture (NICRA), support for agricultural entrepreneurs, development of model 
KVKs, expansion of the KVKs network, the shortage of manpowe r at KVKs, the need

of KVK Hazaribagh, harmful effects of pesticides, the overuse of fertilizers, measures 
to control the sale of banned fertilizers, ensuring the ava ilability of bio -compost and 
other agricultural nutrients at affordable prices. Other concerns included the promotion 
of nano -fertilizers, lack of incentives and challenges faced by farmers in adopting 
organic farming, simplifying the certification process  for organic produce, the 
establishment of the new KVKs, and the strengthening of existing KVKs through 
increased funding, enhancing KVK outreach efforts to farmers, and improving the 
service conditions of KVK employees, etc.

INTRODUCTION 
  
     I, the Chairperson of the Committee on Estimates, having been authorized 
by the Committee to submit the Report on their behalf, do present this Seventh 
Report on the subject ‘Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha 
Evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (PM-KUSUM) & PM Surya Ghar : Muft Bijli Yojana’. 
2.  The PM-KUSUM a flagship scheme of the Government was launched in the 
year 2019 with the objective of providing financial support to farmers for 
solarization of their agriculture water pumps and also to enable farmers to generate 
additional income through installation of solar power plant on their barren land. 
3.  The PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (PMSG: MBY), another flagship 
scheme of the Government was introduced in the year 2024, with the objective of 
providing Rooftop Solar panel system to 1 crore households across the country 
and to empower such households to generate their own electricity. The scheme is 
to be implemented till the end of the FY 2026-27. 
4.  In the aforesaid backdrop, the Committee on E stimates (2024-25) selected 
the subject ‘Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha Evam Utthaan 
Mahabhiyan (PM -KUSUM) & PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana’ for in -depth 
examination on the progress made in implementation of the two schemes and 
report to the House. The Committee on Estimates (2025 -26) continued with 
examination of the subject. 
5.  In this Report, the Committee have undertaken a comprehensive 
examination of various aspects in the process of implementation of PM -KUSUM 
and PMSGY: MBY Sc hemes. With regard to  PM-KUSUM, the Committee have 
dealt with issues like performance of various components of the Scheme, 
provisions of Central Financial Assistance, availability of loans, evacuation of 
power, adoption of Agrivoltaics and need for involvement of public representatives 
in the process of implementation. Further, on PMSG: MBY, the Committee have 
dealt on Challenges in implementation, processing of loans, availability of solar 
module, need for strengthening supply chain network, need for adopt ing the 
concept of model solar city, need for inclusion of the Scheme under the purview of 
DISHA and synchronizing PMSGY & PMAY.   The Committee have analyzed these 
issues/points in detail and have made observations/recommendations in the 
Report.

Introduction  
 
1.1 Energy is acknowledged as a key input towards raising the standard of living of 
citizens of any country, as is evident from the correlation between per capita electricity 
(a proxy for all energy forms) consumption and Human Development Index (HDI).  
Accordingly, energy policies of India have over the years directly aimed to raise per 
capita energy (and electricity) consumption, even while the main focus of the country’s 
development agenda has been on eradication of poverty. 
1.2 India has growing energy need s. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable 
Development also includes a dedicated and stand-alone goal on energy, SDG 7, which 
calls for countries  to "ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern 
energy for all". India’s Human Development Index currently stands at 0.644.25 Based 
on various forms of energy mixes and energy efficiency scenarios, it is estimated that 
the minimum level of per capita final energy requirement for India to become a  
developed country with an HDI of 0.9 must be in the range of 45.7 to 75 gigajoules per 
year. As per the Energy Statistics of India 2024, provisional estimates indicate that the 
total final consumption of energy per capita for FY23 was 16,699 mega joules or16.7 
gigajoules (~approx.),27 indicating that the gap betw een actual and required future  
energy consumption to fuel growth to achieve Viksit Bharat status is quite huge.  
1.3 One of the key pillars of SDG7 is the expansion of renewable energy; however, 
it is clear that even in the most advanced economies, the tec hnologies for renewable 
energy and their implementation are not yet at a maturity level that allows them to fully 
replace fossil fuel-based power plants. Several challenges hinder renewable energy's 
cost-effective and efficient integration into the energy mix. These include significant 
investments required for grid integration, the development of battery infrastructure to 
manage intermittency, scaling up production of the components of renewable energy 
systems, access to critical minerals that are needed for storage technology, the limited 
availability of land in densely populated areas and the competing and rapidly 
increasing energy demands from agriculture, infrastructure, and industry.

Policies and Regulation for the Growth of Renewable Energy in India. 
1.8 When asked to furnish details of Policies and Regulation for the Growth of 
Renewable Energy in India, the Ministry New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) stated 
that India’s renewable energy growth is guided by policies emphasizing local 
manufacturing, financial support particularly for decentralized Re systems, ensuring 
electricity off take and attracting investments. These include: 
a) National Renewable Energy Targets and Frameworks: India aims to achieve 
500 GW of non -fossil capacity by 2030, including ambitious goals for solar, 
wind, and hybrid power systems. Annual tenders for 50 GW of renewable 
capacity ensure a steady pipeline of projects. 
b) Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPOs): Separate RPO trajectories are 
defined for centralized and decentralized renewable sources, promoting large 
scale and household/ farm level deployments. 
c) National Green Hydrogen Mission: Launched in J anuary 2023, it aims to 
position India as a leader in green hydrogen production. The mission targets at 
least 5 million metric tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2030, supported 
by 125 GW of renewable capacity, fostering energy security and job creation. 
d) Domestic Manufacturing and PLI Scheme: The Production Linked Incentive 
(PLI) scheme for high -efficiency solar modules drives domestic solar 
manufacturing, reducing reliance on imports. India aims to scale solar 
manufacturing to 100 GW by 2027. 
e) Infrastructure and Transmission Incentives: The Green Energy Corridor 
Scheme facilitate the smooth transmission of renewable energy and Inter-State 
Transmission System (ISTS) charge waiver helps in reducing project costs and 
improving grid integration until 2032 for offshore wind and 2030 for green 
hydrogen projects.

f) Support for innovative technologies: Wind Solar Hybrid Projects, Floating 
Solar, and Offshore Wind Energy: New initiatives such as floating solar 
systems, wind solar hybrid projects and offshore wind energy projects increase 
the technological base available for RE capacity addition and  achieve target 
of 500 GW by 2030.  
g) Ease of Doing Business and Transparency Measures: The launch of a National 
Solar Rooftop Portal simplifies installation processes, while initiatives like the 
Green Term Ahead Market (GTAM) promote short -term trading of renewable 
power. 
h) Citizen Centric Programmes: PM-KUSUM and PMSGY: PM-KUSUM supports 
farmers with solarized pumps and small solar plants, while the PM Surya Ghar 
Muft Bijli Yojana provides subsidies to households for solar rooftop systems. 
These schemes target to add around 60 GW solar capacity and bring in direct 
citizen participation in the RE growth story.

1.10 Electricity is an essential requirement for all facets of our life.  It has been 
recognized as a basic human need.  It is a critical infrastructure on which the socio -
economic development of the country depends. Supply of electricity at reasonable rate 
to rural India is essential for its overall development.  Equally important is availability 
of reliable and quality power at competitive rates to Indian industry to make it globally 
competitive and enable it to exploit the tremendous potential of employment 
generation.  Services sector has made significant contribution to the growth of our 
economy.  Availability of quality supply of electricity is very crucial to sustained growth 
of this segment.   
1.11 India, being a middle income country, has been subsidizin g agriculture and 
domestic electricity consumers for decades. Subsidization of electricity for agriculture 
started taking place in the 1970s and 1980s as part of the Green Revolution to help 
aid food production in India. The direct translation of this was distribution of highly 
subsidized electricity in the form of flat electricity rates for agriculture or completely 
free agricultural supply.  
1.12 While this subsidization of electricity was successful in increasing food security, 
the formation of the water –energy–food nexus led to adverse impacts. Many of the 
connections under this supply were unmetered, resulting in high consumption of highly 
subsidized energy to irrigate farmers’ lands. Additionally, most of this free energy was 
produced through coal, lea ding to an increase in carbon emissions as more farmers 
opted for irrigation pump-sets to irrigate their land throughout the year. 
1.13 Increasing use of diesel/electric irrigation pumps sets by farmers led to 
depleting groundwater levels as farmers starte d growing more water -intensive crops 
in water-scarce areas as per  Central Groundwater Board (CGWB) Report, 17 per cent 
of India’s groundwater blocks are over-exploited, with 5 per cent and 14 per cent being 
at critical or semi -critical stages. Another con sequence of the same was increasing 
subsidy bids on electricity and financial losses for the DISCOMs despite cross 
subsidizing electricity. Electricity subsidies make up a large share of subsidies in the 
country.

Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (PM-KUSUM) scheme in 2019 with a vision to 
solarize agriculture in India. The scheme, with its components, gives farmers access 
to reliable irrigation technology and provides them with an extra in come source 
through its various components. For domestic consumers, central government has 
factors PM Surya Ghar: Muftbijli Yojana (PMSG:MBY) to increase the share of  solar 
rooftop facility and empower residential household to generate their own electricity.

CHAPTER- II 
PRADHAN MANTRI KISAN URJA SURAKSHA EVAM  UTTHAAN MAHABHIYAN 
(PM-KUSUM)  
2.1 The Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam  Utthaan Mahabhiyan  (PM-
KUSUM) was introduced in 2019 with the objectives of incorporating renewable energy 
in farmers’ irrigation practices; helping farmers gain access to  solar water -pumps at 
subsidized rates; and giving farmers an avenue to utilize their barren land thro ugh 
setting up of solar power plants for energy generation.  
2.2 PM-KUSUM was divided into three components, A, B and C, with 
corresponding targets to be met by 2022. Component A entailed developing solar 
power plants between capacities 500 kW to 2 MW with  the objective of selling 
generated electricity to the DISCOMs. The target for the same was set at 10,000 MW 
of decentralized ground/ stilt -mounted grid -connected solar or other renewable - 
energy-based power plants. Component B includes installation of off -grid solar water 
pumps on farmers’ lands. The target for Component B was set at 17.50 lakh stand -
alone solar agriculture pumps. Component C first entailed solarization of grid -
connected agricultural pumps through installation of grid -connected solar water -
pumps on farmers’ lands. The 2019 target for the same was solarization of 10 lakh 
grid-connected agriculture pumps. 
2.3 Components A and C were supposed to be implemented initially on pilot mode 
for 1,000 MW capacity and one lakh grid -connected agriculture pumps respectively 
while Component B was to be implemented in a full-fledged manner with total Central 
government support of Rs 19,036.5 crore. The scheme was scaled up from its pilot 
stage in 2021, and was in August 2022 extended till 2026. 
2.4 In 2020, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) introduced feeder- 
level solarization (FLS) as a sub -component under Component C in addition to 
solarization of existing electric pumps (to be referred to as individual pump solarization 
or IPS). It revised the targets under Components B and C in January 2024. No change 
in target was proposed for Component A, which remains 10,000 MW to be met by 
2026. The targets for Component B were revised from 17.50 lakh to 14 lakh standalone 

10 
 
solar agriculture pumps. The target for Component C was revised from 10 lakh to 35 
lakh grid-connected agriculture pumps, including feeder level solarization.

Various components of scheme are as follows: - 
i) Component-A: 10,000 MW of Decentralized Ground Mounted Grid Connected 
Solar Power Plants. 
Under this component, farmers can start a solar power plant between capacities 500 
kW and 2 MW and sell the electricity generated to the grid. The Component A benefits 
farmers by giving them access to an extra source of income from their barren land.  
ii) Component-B: Installation of 14 lakh standalone Solar Powered Agriculture 
Pumps. 
Under this component,  farmers can opt for standalone solar water pumps replacing 
their electric/diesel pumps, which would lead to savings in terms of operational costs 
such as amount spent on purchasing diesel or paying electricity bills. Component B 

11 
 
targets small farmers who are currently dependent on the erratic main grid agricultural 
supply.  
iii) Component-C: Solarisation of 35 Lakh Grid-connected Agriculture Pumps. 
Component C is divided into two sub -components. The first is individual pump 
solarization (IPS), which involve s setting up grid -connected solar water -pumps on 
farmers’ lands. Under IPS, the capacity of the solar power plant can be twice the 
capacity of the farmers’ existing water pumps in kW so that farmers can sell the excess 
electricity generated back to the gri d. The second sub -component, feeder - level 
solarization (FLS) in which States are supported for solarization of agriculture feeder 
or mixed feeders. This would help ease the subsidy burden from the state government 
with regard to the subsidy provided to the feeders’ agricultural users. 
Central Financial Assistance (CFA) provisions under the Scheme 
2.6 In order to encourage  implementation, the PM KUSUM scheme envisage 
following provision of Central Financial Assistance: - 
(i) Under Component A, no CFA is provided. However, Procurement Based 
Incentives @ Rs. 0.40 per unit for five years is provided to DISCOMs. 
(ii) Under Component B and Component C (IPS) CFA of 30% of the benchmark 
cost issued by MNRE or the prices of the systems discovered in the tender, 
whichever is lower is provided. However, in North Eastern States including 
Sikkim, Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, 
Lakshadweep and A&N Islands, CFA of 50% of the benchmark cost issued by 
MNRE or the prices of the systems discovered in the tender, whichever is lower, 
is provided. 
(iii) Under Component C (FLS,) for agriculture feeder solarization, CFA of Rs 
1.05 Crore per MW is provided. There is no mandatory requirement of financial 
support from participating State/UT. The feeder so larisation can be 
implemented in CAPEX or RESCO mode.
